ImageDescription.value:
This is a part of a series of drawings of the individual elements electron configuration: Each diagram shows the electron shells with the number of electrons, and furthermore, each electron bears a letter "s", "p", "d" or "f" which shows the orbital electrons belong.

This drawing depicts electron configuration in a atom: The big ball in the middle depicts the nucleus, and the little balls are electrons.

The color on the big ball in the middle is green for non-metals, blue for the noble gases, violet for actinoids, purple pink for transition metals, red alkali metals, gray for "other metals", yellow for halogens, orange for the alkaline earth metal arts and brown for half metals.

ImageDescription.value:
Palladium (Pd) is # 46 on the Periodic Table of Elements. Elemental palladium is a silvery-gray metal. It is one of the platinum-group elements (PGEs; or platinum-group metals, PGMs). Palladium-bearing minerals are rare - it is usually mixed with other PGEs. Palladium-rich minerals famously occur in Montana's Stillwater Complex. Johns-Manville Reef rocks in the Stillwater have intercumulate sulfides such as chalcopyrite and pyrrhotite that are Pd-rich. Occasionally, a Pd-dominant mineral occurs there, such as braggite ((Pt,Pd,Ni)S, platinum palladium nickel sulfide).

Forty-two isotopes of palladium are known - seven occur naturally. Palladium-105, palladium-106, and palladium-108 are each between 20 and 30% of a given Pd sample. Palladium-102, palladium-104, and palladium-110 occur in minor to small amounts. Palladium-107 is radioactive and occurs in trace amounts only.
